extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and researchers interested in misinformation and fake-news websites
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and characterize networks of fake/junk news websites by their operational patterns, content practices, monetization, and linking infrastructure. Useful for journalists, researchers, or platforms investigating coordinated low-quality news sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarized content with updated publish dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, the sites started with plagiarized news from other sites, with updated publish dates, to gain credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the network include sites that copied content from CNN Digital and the Miami Herald. Look for near-verbatim republishing, copied by-lines, or content that matches established outlets but with a newer/altered publish date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of press releases and other secondary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: They would then add press releases and other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators mix plagiarized reporting with press releases and other easily acquired material to bulk up content and appear more diverse/legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featured in Google News and monetized with ad networks
rubrics_metrics.description: These would then be featured in Google News and be monetized with Google AdSense and other schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence in aggregator services and use of common ad monetization platforms (AdSense) are part of the playbook; inclusion in Google News may be used to drive traffic and ad revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical topical orientation: local or finance
rubrics_metrics.description: Content was typically locally oriented or related to finance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many sites present as local news outlets (community names, local beats) or as finance/stock-focused sites. Topic choice is tactical: local content can appear authoritative; finance content can be monetized via affiliate/newsletter signups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fake editor names and claimed owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sites had fake names for editors or claimed to be owned by a nonexistent person named Scott Gentry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check mastheads and ownership statements; invented editor names or nonexistent owners indicate deceptive provenance and reduce credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared technical and commercial infrastructure linking sites
rubrics_metrics.description: The links between the sites were discovered through shared whois records, advertising accounts, web tracking accounts, and other methods, which were linked to a Destin, Florida address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whois data, ad/accounts, and tracking IDs to detect networks. Reused infrastructure (same registrant address, same ad accounts, shared tracking IDs) is a strong indicator of coordination or common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization via affiliate programs and newsletter signups
rubrics_metrics.description: MarketBeat, a financial media company, paid the McGorty sites for newsletter signups as part of its affiliate program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliate payments, paid newsletter signups, or referral arrangements are common revenue streams. Financial incentives can explain churn of low-quality or plagiarized content; check for affiliate links/forms and referral parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: False locality claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites claimed to be based in specific towns (e.g., Richland Standard claimed Bedford, Texas; River Dale Standard claimed Buckner, Kentucky) though these claims were misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local address/claim checks: verify that listed city, offices, or local staff actually exist. Fabricated locality is used to feign community reporting and mislead audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying content from major outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Several sites copied content from established outlets such as the Associated Press, The Journal News, and the Washington Post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for verbatim passages, lifted reporting, or unattributed republishing of major outlets. Repeated copying of named reputable sources signals junk-news behavior rather than legitimate aggregation with attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform enforcement as corroborating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Google News terminated AdSense accounts used by the websites and tuned Google News to not show its content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions by platforms (removal from aggregators, termination of ad accounts) can corroborate that a site is low-quality or violating policies. Use platform responses as one piece of evidence when assessing site legitimacy.
